butir.teks: Damra said, "I said to Sufyan ath-Thawri, 'Do we face the storyteller?' He said, 'Turn your backs on innovations.'" Ibn 'Awn said, "I went in to see Ibn Sirin, and he said, 'What news was there today?' I said, 'The emir forbade the storytellers to tell stories.' He said, 'He was granted success in what is right.'"

Al-A'mash entered the congregational mosque of Basra and saw a storyteller telling stories and saying, "Al-A'mash narrated to us." He went into the middle of the circle and began plucking the hair of his armpit. The storyteller said, "Old man, are you not ashamed?" He said, "Why should I be? I am in a sunna while you are in a lie. I am al-A'mash, and I never narrated to you." Ahmad said, "The people who lie most are the storytellers and the beggars."
'Ali (may Allah be pleased with him) expelled the storytellers from the congregational mosque of Basra.

When he heard the words of al-Hasan al-Basri, he did not expel him, since he was speaking about the knowledge of the Hereafter, reflection on death, drawing attention to the faults of the self, the afflictions of deeds, and the passing thoughts of Satan and the way to be on guard against them. He called to mind the favours and blessings of Allah and the servant's shortcoming in thanking Him, and made known the pettiness of this world, its faults, its passing, its breaking of its covenant, and the danger of the Hereafter and its terrors. This is the reminding (tadhkir) that is praiseworthy in the Law, the encouragement to which is reported in the hadith of Abu Dharr (may Allah be pleased with him), where he said, "Attending a gathering of remembrance is better than praying a thousand rak'as, attending a gathering of knowledge is better than visiting a thousand sick people, and attending a gathering of knowledge is better than being present at a thousand funerals." It was said, "O Messenger of Allah, and than reciting the Qur'an?" He said, "And does reciting the Qur'an benefit except through knowledge?" (١) 'Ata' (may Allah have mercy on him) said, "A gathering of remembrance expiates seventy gatherings of idle amusement." The embellishers have taken these hadiths as proof for vindicating themselves, transferred the name of reminding to their fables, been oblivious to the path of praiseworthy remembrance, and busied themselves with stories which are open to differences, additions, and omissions, and which depart from the stories reported in the Qur'an and add to them. For among stories there are those that are beneficial to hear and those that are harmful, even if true.

Whoever opens that door for himself, truth becomes mixed up for him with falsehood and the beneficial with the harmful. Because of this it was forbidden. Therefore Ahmad ibn Hanbal (may Allah have mercy on him) said, "How much people need a truthful storyteller!" If the story is among the stories of the prophets (peace be upon them) concerning matters of their religion, and the storyteller is truthful and sound in transmission, then I see no harm in it. So let him beware of lying, and of accounts of states that hint at slips or laxities whose meanings the understanding of the common people falls short of grasping, or of grasping that it is a rare slip followed by reflections that make amends through good deeds which cover it. For the layman clings to that in his laxities and slips and prepares an excuse for himself in it, and argues that he related such and such about some shaykhs and some great ones: "We are all prone to acts of disobedience, so it is no wonder if I disobey Allah Most High, for one greater than I has disobeyed Him." That gives him boldness against Allah Most High without his realizing it. So once these two pitfalls are guarded against, there is no harm in it, and at that point he returns to the praiseworthy stories, to what the Qur'an contains, and to the reports that are sound in the authentic books. Some people deem it permissible to fabricate accounts that encourage obedience, and claim that their aim in them is to call people to the truth. This is among the promptings of Satan, for in truthfulness there is ample room to do without lying, and in what Allah Most High and His Messenger (peace and blessings be upon him) mentioned there is sufficiency without invention in preaching. How could it be otherwise, when he disliked laboured rhymed prose and counted it among affectation?

Sa'd ibn Abi Waqqas (may Allah be pleased with him) said to his son 'Umar, when he heard him using rhymed prose, "This is what makes you hateful to me. I will never fulfil your need until you repent" (he had come to him with a need). And the Prophet (peace and blessings be upon him) said to 'Abd Allah ibn Rawaha, who used rhymed prose of three words, "Beware of rhymed prose, O son of Rawaha" (٢). So it seems that the objectionable, laboured rhymed prose is what exceeds two words. And so when the man said concerning the blood-money for the fetus, "How are we to pay blood-money for one who neither drank nor ate nor cried out nor wailed, and the like of that is nullified?", the Prophet (peace and blessings be upon him) said, "Rhymed prose like the rhymed prose of the Bedouins?" (٣)
As for poetry, making much of it in sermons is blameworthy.

Allah Most High says, ⟦QS 26:224-225⟧ And Allah Most High says, ⟦QS 36:69⟧ Most of what preachers are accustomed to in poetry relates to the description of passionate love, the beauty of the beloved, the delight of union, and the pain of separation, while the gathering contains only coarse common people whose inner selves are loaded with appetites and whose hearts are not free from turning to beautiful forms. So the poems stir in their hearts only what lies latent

In them the fires of appetites blaze up, so they shout and work themselves into ecstasy. Most of this, or all of it, goes back to some kind of corruption. So of poetry only that should be used which contains an admonition or a wisdom, by way of citing evidence and for comfort.

The Prophet (peace and blessings be upon him) said, "Some poetry is indeed wisdom" (١). And if the gathering contained the elect, those whose hearts are known to be absorbed in the love of Allah Most High, with none besides them, then poetry whose outward sense points to creatures does no harm among them. For the listener applies everything he hears to whatever overwhelms his heart, as the verification of that will come in the Book of Listening (Kitab as-sama'). For that reason al-Junayd (may Allah have mercy on him) used to speak to a few more than ten men; if they became many, he did not speak, and the people of his gathering never reached twenty.

A group came to the door of the house of Ibn Salim, and it was said to him, "Speak, for your companions have come." He said, "No, these are not my companions; they are only the companions of the gathering. My companions are the elect." As for shath (ecstatic utterance), by it we mean two kinds of speech that some of the Sufis originated.

The first is long, broad claims about passionate love with Allah Most High, and about union that dispenses with outward works, until some people end up claiming unification (ittihad), the lifting of the veil, witnessing through vision, and conversing face to face through address. So they say, "It was said to us such and such, and we said such and such", and in this they imitate al-Husayn ibn Mansur al-Hallaj, who was crucified for uttering words of this kind. They cite as evidence his saying, "I am the Truth", and what is related about Abu Yazid al-Bistami, that he said, "Glory be to me, glory be to me." This is a kind of speech whose harm to the common people is great, so that a group of farmers abandoned their farming and displayed claims of this sort. For this speech is relished by natural inclination, since it contains idleness from works together with vindication of the self through attaining stations (maqamat) and states (ahwal). So the dull-witted are not unable to claim that for themselves, nor to snatch up jumbled, embellished phrases. And whenever this is objected to in them, they are not unable to say, "This is an objection whose source is knowledge and disputation, and knowledge is a veil and disputation is the work of the self, while this talk shines forth only from within, through the unveiling of the light of the Truth." This and the like of it, whose sparks have flown through the lands and whose harm has grown great among the common people, is such that whoever utters anything of it, killing him is better in the religion of Allah than giving life to ten. As for Abu Yazid al-Bistami (may Allah have mercy on him), what is related of him is not sound; and if that was heard from him, perhaps he was relating it from Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, in speech he repeated to himself, as if he were heard saying ⟦QS 20:14⟧, for that was not to be understood from him except by way of relating.

The second kind of shath is unintelligible words that have pleasing outward appearances and contain awe-inspiring expressions, yet there is nothing of substance behind them. Either they are not understood even by their speaker, but he utters them out of confusion in his intellect and disorder in his imagination, due to his scant grasp of the meaning of speech that struck his ear, and this is the most common case

Or they are understood by him, but he is unable to make them understood and to put them in an expression that indicates what is in his mind, due to his scant practice of knowledge and not having learned the way of expressing meanings in elegant words. There is no benefit in this kind of speech, except that it confuses hearts, bewilders minds, and perplexes thoughts, or leads to understanding from it meanings that were not intended by it, each person's understanding being according to his caprice (hawa) and temperament.

The Prophet (peace and blessings be upon him) said, "None of you speaks to a people with a hadith they do not comprehend but it becomes a trial for them" (٢). And the Prophet (peace and blessings be upon him) said, "Speak to people according to what they know and leave what they reject. Do you want Allah and His Messenger to be called liars?" (٣) This applies to what its speaker understands but the intellect of the listener does not reach; so what of what its speaker himself does not understand?
If the speaker understands it but the listener does not, it is not lawful to mention it.
And Jesus said

(peace be upon him): "Do not place wisdom with those who are not its people, for you would wrong it, and do not withhold it from its people, for you would wrong them. Be like the gentle physician who places the medicine at the place of the ailment."

In another wording: "Whoever places wisdom with those who are not its people has acted in ignorance, and whoever withholds it from its people has done wrong. Wisdom has a right and it has people, so give everyone who has a right his right."

As for tamat, what we mentioned about shath applies to them, and there is another matter particular to them: turning the words of the Law away from their understood outward senses to inward matters from which no benefit first occurs to the minds, like the practice of the Batinites in their interpretations. This too is forbidden, and its harm is great. For when words are turned away from what their outward senses require, without holding fast in that to a report from the Lawgiver and without any necessity calling to it from rational proof, that necessitates the loss of trust in words, and the benefit of the speech of Allah Most High and the speech of His Messenger (peace and blessings be upon him) falls away. For what first occurs to the understanding from it cannot be trusted, and the inward meaning has no restraint; rather, passing thoughts conflict in it, and it can be applied in various ways. This too is among the widespread innovations of great harm. Their proponents aim only at the strange, because souls incline to the strange and relish it. By this way the Batinites reached the demolition of the whole Law, by interpreting its outward senses and applying them to their opinion, as we related of their doctrines in the book al-Mustazhiri, composed in refutation of the Batinites.

An example of the interpretation of the people of tamat is what one of them said in interpreting His saying, Most High, ⟦QS 20:24⟧ that it is an allusion to his heart, and he said that this is what is meant by Pharaoh, which is the tyrant over every human being.
And in His saying, Most High, ⟦QS 28:31⟧ that is, whatever he leans on and relies on besides Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, so he ought to cast it away.

And in the saying of the Prophet (peace and blessings be upon him), "Take the pre-dawn meal, for in the pre-dawn meal there is blessing" (١), he meant by it seeking forgiveness in the pre-dawn hours, and the like of that, until they distort the Qur'an from beginning to end away from its outward sense and from its exegesis transmitted from Ibn Abbas and the rest of the scholars. Some of these interpretations are known to be false with certainty, like applying Pharaoh to the heart, for Pharaoh is a perceptible person, the transmission of whose existence and of Moses' call to him has reached us by mass transmission, like Abu Jahl, Abu Lahab, and other disbelievers, and he is not of the kind of satans and angels, which are not perceived by the senses, so that interpretation could enter into the words that mention them. Likewise taking the pre-dawn meal to mean seeking forgiveness, for the Prophet (peace and blessings be upon him) used to take food and say, "Take the pre-dawn meal" (٢) and "Come to the blessed meal" (٣). These are matters whose falsity is perceived through mass transmission and the senses, by way of transmission, while some are known to be false by preponderant conjecture, and that is in matters not connected with sensation. All of that is forbidden, a misguidance, and a corruption of the religion for people. Nothing of this was transmitted from the Companions, nor from the Followers, nor from al-Hasan al-Basri, despite his devotion to calling people and preaching to them. So no meaning appears for the saying of the Prophet (peace and blessings be upon him), "Whoever interprets the Qur'an by his opinion, let him take his seat in the Fire" (٤), except this type: that his aim and opinion is to establish and substantiate a matter, so he drags the testimony of the Qur'an toward it and applies it to it, without any verbal, linguistic, or transmitted indication testifying to applying it to it. It should not be understood from it that the Qur'an must not be interpreted by deduction and reflection, for some verses have five, six, and seven meanings transmitted about them from the Companions and the exegetes.

We know that none of these was heard from the Prophet (peace and blessings be upon him), for they may be mutually contradictory and not admit of being combined, so that is something deduced through good understanding and long reflection. For this reason the Prophet (peace and blessings be upon him) said to Ibn Abbas (may Allah be pleased with him), "O Allah, give him understanding in the religion and teach him interpretation" (٥).

Whoever among the people of tamat deems such interpretations permissible while knowing that they are not what the words intend, and claims that he aims thereby to call creation to the Creator, resembles one who deems it permissible to invent and fabricate against the Messenger of Allah (peace and blessings be upon him) something that is true in itself but which the Law did not state, like one who fabricates for every issue he sees as true a hadith from the Prophet (peace and blessings be upon him). That is wrongdoing, misguidance, and entry into the threat understood from the saying of the Prophet (peace and blessings be upon him), "Whoever lies about me deliberately, let him take his seat in the Fire" (١). Rather, the evil in interpreting these words is more calamitous and greater, because they displace trust in words and cut off entirely the way to benefit and understanding from the Qur'an. You have now learned how Satan turned people's motives from the praiseworthy sciences to the blameworthy ones; all of that comes from the deception of the scholars of evil through the changing of names. If you follow these people relying on the famous name, without regard to what was known in the first age, you would be like one who sought honour through wisdom by following one called a sage, for the name sage has come to be applied to the physician, the poet, and the astrologer in this age, and that is through heedlessness of the changing of words. The fifth word is wisdom (hikma), for the name sage has come to be applied to the physician, the poet, and the astrologer, even to the one who rolls the gourd on the palms of the villagers in the thoroughfares of the roads.

Wisdom is what Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, praised, saying Most High, ⟦QS 2:269⟧ And the Prophet (peace and blessings be upon him) said, "A word of wisdom that a man learns is better for him than this world and what is in it" (٢). So look at what wisdom was an expression for and to what it was transferred, measure the rest of the words by it, and guard against being deluded by the deceptions of the scholars of evil, for their evil to the religion is greater than the evil of the satans, since Satan, through them, proceeds gradually to pull the religion out of people's hearts. For this reason, when the Messenger of Allah (peace and blessings be upon him) was asked about the worst of creation, he refused and said, "O Allah, forgive," until they repeated it to him, and then he said, "They are the scholars of evil" (٣). You have now learned the praiseworthy and the blameworthy knowledge and the source of the confusion, and the choice is yours to look to yourself and follow the early generations (salaf), or to dangle by the rope of delusion and imitate the later generations (khalaf). Every science that the early generations approved of has been effaced, and most of what people devote themselves to is innovated and newly introduced. The saying of the Messenger of Allah (peace and blessings be upon him) is sound: "Islam began as a stranger and will return as a stranger as it began, so glad tidings to the strangers." It was said, "Who are the strangers?" He said, "Those who put right what people have corrupted of my sunna, and those who revive what they have caused to die of my sunna" (٤). In another: "They are those who hold fast to what you are on today" (٥). In another hadith: "The strangers are a few righteous people among many people; those who hate them among people are more than those who love them" (٦). Those sciences have become strange, such that whoever mentions them is detested. For this reason ath-Thawri (may Allah have mercy on him) said, "When you see a scholar with many friends, know that he is one who mixes, because if he speaks the truth they will hate him."
